title: Questions
description: Ask yes-or-no questions three ways: intonation, est-ce que and inversion.

guide.summary: A yes-or-no question can be asked three ways: with your voice alone, with est-ce que, or by putting the verb in front of the pronoun. This topic gives you all three, plus negative questions and the special yes they need.

sections.title: Which of the three ways?
sections.text: All three ask exactly the same yes-or-no question; only the style changes. Inversion sounds careful and is common in writing, while everyday speech uses the voice or est-ce que. When a task does not name a form, any of the three is accepted.
steps: Read the task: it usually names the way to use.
Intonation: keep the statement as it is and add a question mark.
Est-ce que: put the opening in front and change nothing else.
Inversion: move the subject pronoun behind the verb, with a hyphen.

examples.fr: Est-ce que tu pars ce week-end ?

watch: An intonation question adds nothing at all: “Vous parlez-vous anglais ?” mixes two ways in one sentence.
Never put inversion after est-ce que: one way per question.
French leaves a space before the question mark: Pars-tu ?

sections.title: Est-ce que: add an opening, change nothing
sections.text: Est-ce que is a fixed opening. Put it in front of the statement and leave every other word exactly where it was.

rows: Est-ce que la soupe est chaude ?

steps: Write the statement as it is: subject first, verb after it.
Put the opening in front of the whole statement.
Keep a noun group whole — article plus noun — and leave it before its verb.
Finish with a space and a question mark.

examples.fr: Est-ce que le magasin est ouvert ?

watch: Not “Est-ce que parles-tu ?”: after the opening the subject stays in front of its verb.
The opening carries one hyphen, between est and ce.

sections.title: Que or qu’?
sections.text: The final e of que disappears before a vowel sound and an apostrophe takes its place. Nothing else in the sentence changes.
steps: Look at the word that comes straight after the opening.
Vowel sound (il, elle, ils, elles, on, un ami): drop the final e and write an apostrophe against the next word.
Consonant sound (tu, nous, vous, le, la, and the l of l’avion): keep the full form.
watch: The apostrophe replaces the dropped letter: never write que’il.
L’enfant begins with the sound l, so the opening stays whole in front of it.
No space around the apostrophe: qu’ils, written as one block.

sections.title: Inversion: verb first, pronoun after
sections.text: Move the subject pronoun behind the verb and join the two with a hyphen. The rest of the sentence keeps its place.
steps: Conjugate the verb for the subject pronoun, exactly as in the statement.
Write the verb first, then a hyphen, then the pronoun.
Leave the rest of the sentence untouched.
watch: The hyphen is obligatory: the verb and the pronoun form one written unit.
Inverting never changes the verb ending: with tu the verb keeps its -s.
The pronoun is used once: “Vous parlez-vous” has written it twice.

sections.title: When to add -t-
sections.text: Two vowel sounds cannot meet between the verb and il, elle or on. A -t- is written between two hyphens to keep them apart.
steps: Invert the verb and the pronoun first.
Check the pronoun: only il, elle and on can call for the link.
Check the verb's last letter: a vowel takes -t- between two hyphens; a t or a d takes nothing.

examples.en: Does he listen to the radio?

watch: The link is never glued to the verb (at-il) and never doubled after a t (finit-t-il).
No apostrophe is involved: the letter sits between two hyphens.
With tu, nous, vous, ils and elles the link is never added.

sections.title: Inversion with a noun subject
sections.text: A noun subject does not move. It stays in front, and a pronoun standing for it is added after the verb.
steps: Leave the whole noun group in front of the verb.
Conjugate the verb to agree with that noun.
Add the pronoun matching its gender and number after the verb, with a hyphen.
Put -t- between them when the verb ends in a vowel and the pronoun is il or elle.

examples.en: Do the shops close at noon?

watch: The noun never goes behind the verb in a yes-or-no question: not “Vient Paul ?”.
The added pronoun only repeats the noun; the verb still agrees with the noun.
This is the careful form; est-ce que is easier in speech.

sections.title: Questions in the passé composé
sections.text: In a two-part tense only the helping verb moves. The past participle stays behind the pronoun.

rows: after the pronoun, before the participle

steps: Find the helping verb of the passé composé: a form of avoir or être.
Invert that helper with the pronoun and join them with a hyphen.
Put any short adverb, then the participle, after the pronoun.
Add -t- when the helper ends in a vowel and the pronoun is il, elle or on.
watch: Never hook the pronoun to the participle: not “As mangé-tu ?”.
The participle does not change for the person; only the helper does.
The helper a ends in a vowel, so it takes the link before il and elle.

sections.title: Negative questions, and the yes that contradicts
sections.text: A question can be negative: ne … pas wraps the verb. Saying yes against it takes a word of its own.
steps: Build the question the usual way first.
Put ne before the verb — before the whole verb-pronoun block when it is inverted — and pas after it.
Ne becomes n’ before a vowel or a mute h.
Answering yes against a negative question uses si; oui answers a positive one.

examples.fr: — Tu ne travailles pas ? — Si, je travaille.

watch: Casual speech drops ne (Tu viens pas ?), but writing keeps it.
In inversion pas follows the whole block, never the verb alone.
Non after a negative question agrees with it: it says the thing really is not happening.

Add nothing at the front and move nothing.
Check the subject appears once only, in front of its verb.

Put the opening in front of it and change nothing after it.
Check the pronoun is still before its verb, with no hyphen anywhere.

Leave the noun in front of its verb; it never jumps behind it here.
Look at the first sound of the word that follows the opening.
Vowel sound: drop the final e and write an apostrophe against that word, with no space.
Consonant sound, including the l of l’avion: keep the full form.
Conjugate the verb for the subject pronoun, as in the statement.
Write the verb, then a hyphen, then the pronoun.
Check the verb ending still matches that person.
Invert the verb and the pronoun first.
Only il, elle and on can need the link.
Verb ending in a vowel: write the link between two hyphens. Verb ending in t or d: add nothing.
Leave the noun subject in front of the verb.
Pick the pronoun matching its gender and number.
Attach that pronoun after the verb with a hyphen, adding the link if two vowels would meet.
Find the helping verb: a form of avoir or être.
Invert the helper with the pronoun, joined by a hyphen.
Put any short adverb and then the participle after the pronoun.
Build the question, then wrap ne … pas around the verb, or around the verb-pronoun block.
Shorten ne to n’ before a vowel.
A yes that contradicts a negative question is not the ordinary one.

The noun subject has been pushed behind the verb. A noun does not move in a yes-or-no question; a pronoun is added after the verb instead.
Il stands for a masculine person, so it does not match the name in front.

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct form.
exercises.hint: The pronoun after the verb stands for tes parents, and the verb agrees with it.
exercises.feedback: Check the verb ending and whether a -t- is needed between the verb and ils.
exercises.explanation: Viennent-ils repeats tes parents with ils. Viennent ends in t, so no extra -t- is added.

mistakes.why: The linking letter is only needed to keep two vowels apart, and this verb form already ends in t.
Vient is the singular form. The noun in front is plural, and both the verb and the added pronoun must match it.

exercises.instruction: Fix the inversion. Keep Paul as the first word.
exercises.hint: A noun subject does not move after the verb in a yes-or-no question. A pronoun does.
exercises.feedback: Put Paul back before the verb and add the pronoun that stands for him after it.
exercises.explanation: With a noun subject, keep the noun first and add il after the verb: Paul vient-il ce soir ?

alternatives.answer: Est-ce que Paul vient ce soir ?
alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks you to fix the inversion: Paul vient-il ce soir ?
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks you to fix the inversion: Paul vient-il ce soir ?

mistakes.why: That is the sentence as given, with the noun behind the verb. A noun subject stays in front; only a pronoun may follow the verb.
The extra letter is only needed to separate two vowels, and this verb already ends in t.
The name has to open the question; it cannot trail after the verb and its pronoun.

exercises.instruction: Build the question using inversion with the noun subject.
exercises.source: Does the bus leave at noon?
exercises.hint: Start with le bus, then the verb with the pronoun that stands for it.
exercises.feedback: Two verb tiles look alike. Check whether part needs an extra -t-.
exercises.explanation: Le bus stays first and il is added after part. Part already ends in t, so there is no extra -t-.

mistakes.why: The linking letter separates two vowels, and this verb already ends in t, so nothing is added.
The noun subject has to stay in front of the verb; the pronoun after the verb only repeats it.

exercises.instruction: Write jouer in the present with the inverted pronoun that stands for ta sœur.
exercises.hint: The pronoun for ta sœur is elle, and joue ends in a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Write the verb, a linking letter if two vowels meet, then the pronoun, all with hyphens.
exercises.explanation: Ta sœur is repeated by elle after the verb, with -t- between the vowels: Ta sœur joue-t-elle du piano ?

mistakes.why: The verb ends in a vowel and the pronoun begins with one, so a linking letter has to stand between them.
Il stands for a man. The noun in front is feminine, so the added pronoun must match her.
The verb alone does not ask the question here, and the noun in front is one person: the pronoun repeating it comes after the verb, in the singular.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French using inversion. Start with Léa.

alternatives.answer: Est-ce que Léa aime la mer ?
alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks for inversion.
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: Keep Léa first and repeat her with a pronoun after the verb.
exercises.feedback: Léa stays in front. Check the vowels between aime and the pronoun.
exercises.explanation: Léa is repeated by elle, linked with -t-: Léa aime-t-elle la mer ?

mistakes.why: Two vowels touch between the verb and the pronoun; French puts a linking letter between them.
The name has been dropped, but the task asks the question to start with her; the pronoun after the verb only repeats it.
Il points to a masculine person, and the added pronoun must match the noun it repeats.

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct form.
exercises.hint: The added pronoun must match ta mère, and habite ends in a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Check two things: the pronoun’s gender and the link between two vowels.
exercises.explanation: Ta mère is feminine, so the pronoun is elle, joined with -t-: habite-t-elle.

mistakes.why: The verb ends in a vowel and the pronoun begins with one; without a linking letter the two would collide.
Il stands for a masculine person, and ta mère is feminine, so the pronoun repeating her does not match.

exercises.instruction: Turn this statement into a question using inversion.

alternatives.answer: Est-ce que tu as fini ton café ?
alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks for inversion.
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: In the passé composé, only the auxiliary swaps places with the pronoun.
exercises.feedback: Invert as and tu, and leave the participle after them.
exercises.explanation: The auxiliary as is inverted with tu, and fini follows: As-tu fini ton café ?

mistakes.why: The pronoun has been hooked to the participle. In a two-part past tense only the helping verb swaps with the pronoun.
The pronoun is written twice. Inverting moves it behind the helper instead of adding a second one.
The participle takes no -s here; only the helping verb changes for the person.

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct inverted form.
exercises.hint: Which word is inverted with the pronoun: the auxiliary or the participle?
exercises.feedback: The pronoun joins the auxiliary, and the participle comes after both.
exercises.explanation: As-tu vu inverts the auxiliary as with tu, then adds the participle vu.

mistakes.why: The pronoun is stuck to the participle. It belongs right after the helping verb, the only word that inverts.
The participle has been dragged to the front; it stays at the end of the block, after the pronoun.

exercises.instruction: Write avoir for vous, inverted with a hyphen.
exercises.hint: Invert the auxiliary, not fini.
exercises.feedback: Write the vous form of avoir, then the pronoun, joined by a hyphen.
exercises.explanation: Vous avez fini becomes Avez-vous fini ? The participle stays after the pronoun.

mistakes.why: That is statement order. The task asks for the inverted order, helper first.
The order is right, but the two words must be joined by a hyphen to form one block.
Être is the wrong helper for finir: its passé composé is built with avoir.
Those are other persons. The task names vous, so the helper and the pronoun both have to be that person.

exercises.instruction: Build the question using inversion.
exercises.hint: Start with the auxiliary and pronoun, then the participle.
exercises.feedback: Two auxiliary tiles look alike. Check what goes between a and elle.
exercises.explanation: A and elle are separated by -t-: A-t-elle téléphoné à sa mère ?

mistakes.why: The helper ends in a vowel and the pronoun begins with one, so a linking letter has to separate them.
The participle has been moved to the front; it stays after the helper and its pronoun.

exercises.instruction: Fix the word order in this inverted question.
exercises.hint: The pronoun attaches to the auxiliary, not to the participle.
exercises.feedback: Move vous next to the auxiliary and put the participle after it.
exercises.explanation: In the passé composé, invert the auxiliary and the pronoun: Avez-vous vu mes clés ?

mistakes.why: That is the sentence as given: the pronoun is hooked to the participle, but only the helping verb swaps with the pronoun.
The order is right now, yet the helper and the pronoun are left as two loose words instead of one hyphenated block.
That returns to statement order, so the inversion the task asks you to repair has gone.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French using inversion.

alternatives.answer: Est-ce que vous avez bien dormi ?
alternatives.message: That is a correct question with est-ce que. This exercise asks for inversion.
That is a correct spoken question with rising intonation. This exercise asks for inversion.

exercises.hint: Invert the auxiliary with vous. Short adverbs such as bien go before the participle.
exercises.feedback: Use avoir for vous, invert it, then put bien and dormi after the pronoun.
exercises.explanation: Avez-vous bien dormi ? inverts the auxiliary; bien sits between the pronoun and the participle.

mistakes.why: Bien is a short adverb: it sits between the pronoun and the participle, not after it.
Tu is the friendly you, and the task marks the question as formal.
Dormir builds its passé composé with avoir, not with être.

exercises.instruction: Choose the right reply.
exercises.source: — Tu ne viens pas ? — ____, je viens !
exercises.hint: The reply contradicts a negative question.
exercises.feedback: The speaker is coming, which goes against the question. French has a special yes for that.
exercises.explanation: Si is the yes that contradicts a negative question. Oui answers a positive question, and non would mean the person is not coming.

mistakes.why: Oui agrees with a question asked in the positive. This question was built with ne … pas and the reply pushes back against it, which French marks differently.
Non agrees with the negative question and would mean the speaker is not coming, which contradicts the rest of the reply.

exercises.instruction: Write the one-word reply that contradicts the negative question.
exercises.source: — Vous n’aimez pas le fromage ? — ____, j’adore ça !
exercises.hint: The answer disagrees with a question containing ne…pas.
exercises.feedback: This is a yes, but not the usual one.
exercises.explanation: After a negative question, yes is si: Si, j’adore ça !

mistakes.why: Oui answers a question asked in the positive. Here the question carries n’… pas and the reply goes against it.
Non agrees with the negative question, so it would say the speaker dislikes cheese, while the rest of the reply says the opposite.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
answers: Est-ce que tu n’as pas faim ?

alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech, but written French keeps ne: Tu n’as pas faim ?

exercises.hint: Avoir faim is the French for “to be hungry”. Put the negation around the verb.
exercises.feedback: Use tu with avoir faim and wrap ne…pas around the conjugated verb. Ne becomes n’ before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Tu n’as pas faim ? keeps n’…pas around as. With inversion, the negation wraps the verb and pronoun together: N’as-tu pas faim ?

mistakes.why: Es is être, but French does not say “be hungry”: hunger is something you have, so the verb is avoir.
Ne keeps its vowel only before a consonant. The verb here starts with a vowel, so ne is shortened with an apostrophe.
Avoir faim is a fixed pair: no article comes between the verb and faim.

exercises.instruction: Make this question negative. Keep the inversion.
exercises.hint: The negation wraps around the inverted verb and pronoun as one block.
exercises.feedback: Put ne, shortened before a vowel, before the verb, and pas after the pronoun.
exercises.explanation: In an inverted question, ne goes before aimes-tu and pas after it: N’aimes-tu pas le poisson ?

mistakes.why: Ne cannot keep its vowel in front of another vowel; it is shortened with an apostrophe.
The verb and the pronoun form one block, so nothing may be slipped between them; the second half of the negation follows the whole block.
That puts the pronoun back in front of the verb, dropping the inversion the task asks you to keep.

exercises.instruction: The question was: Il ne travaille pas aujourd’hui ? Fix the reply so it means yes, he is working.
exercises.hint: A yes that answers a negative question is a different word.
exercises.feedback: The rest of the reply is right. Change only the first word.
exercises.explanation: The reply contradicts a negative question, so French uses si instead of oui.

mistakes.why: That is the reply as given. Oui only agrees with a question asked in the positive, and this question carried ne … pas.
Non agrees with the negative question, so it would mean he is not working — the opposite of the rest of the sentence.
Mais only strengthens the word after it, and that word is still the yes used after a positive question.
